title: Pauri 2, meaning: all within the order
hookLine: all forms, high and low, joy and pain, come by the order; whoever understands it no longer says I, I (Japji 2)

lines: I GOT STUCK. I CAN'T BELIEVE IT.
cards: I got stuck in traffic. I had the worst meeting. I can't believe they said that to me.
I, I, I. Nothing wrong with it; that's how stories work.
But when a day goes badly, the I can get so big it fills the whole picture, and everything else, the traffic, the other people, the weather, becomes something that happened to me.
Guru Nanak's second pauri ends by naming that I, and what makes it shrink.

teach.b: Here is the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe.

teach.h: NO ONE IS OUTSIDE THE ORDER.
teach.b: By the order, forms are made; the order can't be described. By the order, living beings come to be; by the order, some are given greatness. By the order some are high and some low; by the order, pain and joy are written.
Some, by the order, are blessed; others, by the order, wander on and on. Everyone is within the order; no one is outside it. Then the last line: Nanak, whoever understands the order doesn't say I, I.
The word there is haumai. Hau means I. Mai means me.
I-me. You met it in camp three, as the ego that loves credit for its seva. Here it's bigger: the habit of standing outside everything, as if the world were happening to you alone.
Sikh teaching names haumai as a deep trouble.

teach.h: THE CURE IS INSIDE IT TOO.
teach.b: Guru Angad, in a salok later in the Granth, calls it, in paraphrase, a long, deep illness, and then says the cure is inside it too. That's the hope the pauri holds out.
If everything, high and low, joy and pain, is within the order, then no one stands outside it keeping score; each person is in it, with everyone else.
Read that way, the traffic, the meeting and the rude remark are within the order too.
That doesn't mean everything is fine, or that nothing should change; Sikh teaching also asks for honest work and standing against injustice.
It means, in the pauri's terms, that the I stops being the center of the map, and the constant I, I goes quiet.

how: Sikhs recite the second pauri each morning; haumai, ego, is named in the Guru Granth Sahib as a deep obstacle, and seva, simran and sangat are the everyday ways of thinning it.

o: I-me, the ego that stands outside everything
a small drum played while the hymns are sung
a cold morning bath taken before the prayers

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.
p: high and low, pain and joy
a deep illness, with its cure inside

s: pauri two says some people live outside the order
everyone is within the order; no one is outside it.
understanding the order means nothing should ever change
Sikh teaching also asks for honest work and standing against injustice; the I just stops being the center of the map.
the pauri ends by naming haumai
whoever understands the order doesn't say I, I.

games.q: the pauri says some are high, some low, some blessed, some wandering, all by the order. what does it say about the one who understands this?
o: they become the highest of all.
they no longer say I, I.
games.why: Nanak, whoever understands the order doesn't speak in haumai.

practice: Find one moment from today or yesterday when the I got big: a complaint, a grudge, a time the world seemed to be happening to you.

Now widen the picture: who else was there, what were they carrying, what else was going on, the weather, the hour, the tiredness, until you're one person among many. Breathe there, inside it; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Haumai. I-me: the ego that stands outside everything. Japji's second pauri says it goes quiet when the order is understood.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: haumai, I-me, the ego. hau, I, and mai, me.

carryVoice: Your line: all within the order. Hau, I; mai, me; and all around them, everyone else. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Angad on haumai)
Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 2
